q-12019.solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 3(@@L@@)^{-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=@@L@@.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3(@@L@@)^{-3}\,\text{d}x & =3\int {u}^{-3}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)}{u}^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(@@L@@)^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2(@@L@@)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2(@@L@@)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(@@L@@)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(@@L@@)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)(@@L@@)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@@L@@)+0 \\  & =-(@@L@@)^{-3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =3(@@L@@)^{-3} \\  & =\frac{3}{(@@L@@)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
